title: Plan cryptographic agility and evaluate quantum claims
summary: Cryptographic agility is the governed ability to inventory, choose, replace, and verify cryptographic mechanisms as risks, standards, interoperability, and implementation conditions change. Quantum-related planning should distinguish current exposure, long-lived confidentiality, migration dependencies, and unproven or context-dependent claims.
outcome: Plan justified cryptographic migration and evaluate quantum-related claims by inventorying dependencies, prioritizing exposure, and validating a controlled transition.
managerMindset: Avoid both panic replacement and indefinite inertia. Make a risk-owned roadmap from cryptographic inventory, data longevity, dependency, approved options, test evidence, and rollback criteria.

sections.title: Build the conditions for controlled change
sections.body: Agility begins with an inventory of algorithms, libraries, protocols, certificates, keys, owners, data classifications, interoperability partners, hardware or service dependencies, and expiry dates. Abstracting every detail is not required, but untracked embedded choices make migration difficult. Define approved cryptographic profiles, procurement requirements, change authority, test environments, compatibility plans, telemetry, rollback criteria, and deprecation dates. Treat a change in algorithm, parameter, library, or trust anchor as a controlled architecture and operations change.
keyPoints: You cannot prioritize migration reliably without knowing where cryptography is used and what data it protects.
Agility is governance, engineering, testing, and operations—not only modular code.

sections.title: Separate quantum concepts from unsupported certainty
sections.body: The outline includes quantum among cryptographic methods and quantum key distribution in the PKI context. Quantum computing risk discussions commonly focus on whether certain public-key approaches may face different future feasibility assumptions; the appropriate response depends on data sensitivity and required confidentiality lifetime, not a claim that every system is already broken. Quantum key distribution is a specialized key-establishment approach with physical, operational, integration, and trust assumptions; it is not a universal replacement for PKI, endpoint security, authorization, or key lifecycle management.
keyPoints: Long-lived sensitive data can justify earlier planning even when migration is not immediate.
Quantum-related technology still needs identity, operations, availability, and endpoint controls.

sections.title: Prioritize and validate a transition
sections.body: Rank uses by data longevity, impact, external exposure, migration complexity, supplier support, and assurance evidence. Pilot approved replacement profiles where compatible, test performance and failure behavior, validate certificate and key processes, coordinate partners, and retain a time-bounded rollback plan that does not silently restore a deprecated weak state. Record exceptions with owners and expiration. The successful outcome is verified maintained protection during transition, not merely a list of new algorithm names.
keyPoints: Migration must include partners, devices, libraries, trust anchors, and recovery procedures.
A fallback can be necessary, but it must be constrained and removed deliberately.

sections.title: Use current post-quantum terminology without a universal migration claim
sections.body: NIST finalized FIPS 203 ML-KEM for key establishment in 2024; related final signature standards are FIPS 204 ML-DSA and FIPS 205 SLH-DSA. A standard’s existence does not prove every protocol, partner, device, certificate workflow, or implementation is ready to migrate. Inventory public-key uses and confidentiality/verification lifetime, identify approved profiles and interoperability constraints, then test a governed transition. The failure mode is buying a “quantum-safe” claim without knowing the protocol role, cryptographic boundary, implementation assurance, fallback, or partner support.
keyPoints: ML-KEM establishes a shared secret; it is not a label for every cryptographic function.
Migration priority follows data lifetime, exposure, dependency, and safe deployability.

workedExamples.title: Ten-year legal archive
workedExamples.situation: An organization stores confidential signed records that must remain verifiable for a decade and are exchanged with outside parties.
workedExamples.reasoning: Inventory encryption, signatures, certificate chains, archived validation evidence, libraries, partner constraints, and retention requirements. Prioritize the long-lived confidential archive, choose approved migration profiles through governance, test validation and re-signing or protected archival processes as applicable, coordinate partners, and retain evidence of the transition.
workedExamples.takeaway: Long-lived confidentiality and verifiability make inventory and transition evidence more important than a generic quantum headline.

workedExamples.title: Partner API transition
workedExamples.situation: An organization protects a long-lived data exchange with external partners.
workedExamples.reasoning: Inventory each protocol’s key-establishment and signature functions, certificate/trust path, libraries, hardware, partners, and data lifetime. Pilot an approved compatible profile, test failure and rollback behavior, and retire exceptions on a controlled date.
workedExamples.takeaway: Algorithm names cannot substitute for protocol-role and partner-readiness analysis.

distinctions.difference: Replacement is one technical act; agility is the sustained ability to discover dependencies, govern choices, test, deploy, monitor, recover, and retire cryptographic mechanisms.
Planning considers migration of cryptographic assumptions and implementations; QKD is a specific specialized key-establishment technique with its own deployment assumptions.
ML-KEM is a key-encapsulation mechanism for establishing a shared secret; ML-DSA is a digital-signature algorithm. They serve different protocol roles.

misconceptions.claim: Quantum key distribution eliminates the need for certificates, endpoints, and key management.
misconceptions.correction: It addresses a narrow key-establishment context and still relies on authenticated operational, endpoint, and lifecycle controls.

misconceptions.claim: ML-KEM alone makes a protocol quantum safe.
misconceptions.correction: A protected protocol still needs appropriate authentication/signatures, implementation assurance, endpoint and key management, and an interoperable lifecycle.

recallChecks.prompt: What inventory fields make cryptographic migration actionable?
recallChecks.answer: Use or protocol, algorithm and parameters, owner, data and longevity, keys or certificates, dependencies, interoperability partners, service impact, and approved replacement path.

recallChecks.prompt: Why is a long-lived archive a priority candidate for planning?
recallChecks.answer: Its confidentiality or verifiability needs may outlast current assumptions, so delayed inventory and migration can leave no safe transition window.

recallChecks.prompt: What is the first distinction when evaluating a PQC product claim?
recallChecks.answer: Whether it supplies key establishment, signatures, or another cryptographic function, and where that function sits in the real protocol.

scenarioSeeds.prompt: A procurement team buys a 'quantum-safe' appliance without knowing its protocols or partner compatibility. What should happen first?
scenarioSeeds.decisiveDetail: Inventory the protected uses, data longevity, interfaces, approved profiles, dependencies, assurance evidence, and migration test criteria before selecting a product claim.

scenarioSeeds.prompt: A vendor offers ML-KEM but cannot identify its protocol integration or partner support. What must be established before approval?
scenarioSeeds.decisiveDetail: The protected protocol role, data lifetime, implementation/profile assurance, dependencies, interoperability, migration tests, and rollback/deprecation governance.

studyPlan.learn: Build a small cryptographic inventory including owner, data lifetime, dependency, and replacement constraint.
studyPlan.connect: Connect D1 risk prioritization, D4 protocol interoperability, D5 certificates, D7 change management, and D8 dependency management.
studyPlan.apply: Write a migration acceptance and rollback criterion for one service.
studyPlan.revisit: In three days, distinguish agility from QKD.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: Which cryptographic dependency should move first, and what controlled transition proves it remains protected?
visualLearningContract.misconception: A new PQC standard proves every system is ready to migrate.
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned comparisons force a distinction among scope, selection trigger, concrete failure, and retrieval response.
visualLearningContract.focalInsight: Algorithm names are only one part of an accountable inventory, compatibility, rollout, rollback, and retirement decision.
visualLearningContract.intentionalOmissions: Detailed vendor commands and environment-specific parameters remain in the cited sources and are not implied by this learning view.
visualLearningContract.retrievalPrompt: Given a public-key use, name its role, owner, lifetime, partner constraint, and migration evidence.
